lesson.title: Downhill Lines: Recognizing and Computing Negative Slope
lesson.summary: A negative slope means a line falls from left to right, describing any situation where the output shrinks as the input grows.
lesson.body:
Just as positive slope describes a line climbing uphill from left to right, negative slope describes a line falling downhill from left to right. As the x-coordinate increases, the y-coordinate decreases. If positive slope feels like walking uphill while scanning a graph left to right, negative slope feels like walking downhill.

Negative slope appears whenever more input leads to less output. A tank of water draining over time loses gallons as minutes pass. The remaining balance on a loan being paid off shrinks as more payments are made. The altitude of a hiker descending a trail drops as the distance traveled increases. In each case, one quantity grows while the other quantity shrinks, and that opposite movement produces a negative slope.

Work through an example using the points (0, 10) and (5, negative 5). With x1 = 0, y1 = 10, x2 = 5, y2 = negative 5, the slope formula gives m = (negative 5 minus 10) divided by (5 minus 0), which is negative 15 divided by 5, and that equals negative 3. The slope is negative 3. Looking at the raw coordinates confirms the direction: x increased from 0 to 5, a rise of 5 units to the right, while y dropped from 10 all the way to negative 5, a decrease of 15 units. One coordinate grew while the other fell, exactly the pattern that produces a negative result.

It is worth being precise about what the negative sign means, because it is easy to mix up with the size of the drop. A slope of negative 3 means that for every 1 unit you move to the right, the line falls 3 units. A slope of negative 1/4 would describe a much gentler downhill slide, falling only a quarter of a unit for each unit moved right. Between negative 3 and negative 1/4, the line with slope negative 3 is steeper, because its distance from 0 is larger, even though negative 3 is the smaller number on the number line. When comparing steepness rather than direction, look at the size of the slope, ignoring the sign.

As with positive slope, you can predict the sign before finishing the arithmetic by watching how the coordinates move. If x increases while y decreases, or if x decreases while y increases, the slope will be negative, because dividing a positive by a negative, or a negative by a positive, always produces a negative result. Recognizing this pattern quickly helps you catch a sign error the moment it happens rather than after the whole problem is finished.

The sign shows up immediately in slope-intercept form as well. An equation such as y equals negative 3x plus 10 has slope negative 3, so before plotting anything you already know the line falls from left to right, and you can picture it descending steeply, dropping 3 units for every 1 unit moved right. If a second line instead has slope negative 1/4, it also falls left to right, but far more gradually, dropping only a quarter unit for every unit moved right. Comparing the two, the line with slope negative 3 is the steeper downhill path, even though negative 3 is a smaller number than negative 1/4 on the number line, because steepness compares the size of the slope while direction compares its sign, and the two questions, how steep and which way, are answered separately.
